Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Define basic biomechanics terms, including kinematics, kinetics, degrees of freedom, force,
moment/torque, and free-body diagram.
Explain how the kinematics and kinetics of the hip are related to the structure of the hip joint.
Describe the mechanics of the hip, the pathologic hip, and total hip arthroplasty.
Biomechanics
Biomechanics (Resource 1) is the study of forces and motion on the musculoskeletal system.
Biomechanics combines principles from physics, engineering, and biology (Resource 2).

The application of mechanics, or the study of forces and motion, to the musculoskeletal
system is termed biomechanics. Mechanics is a field of physics that applies Newton’s
laws to understand the manner in which objects react to the forces acting on them. An
understanding of biomechanics, the mechanical basis of musculoskeletal system
function, provides practitioners with knowledge to improve diagnosis and management
and facilitates evaluation and refinement of surgical and nonsurgical management.
Statics and Dynamics
Mechanics can be divided into the study of objects and systems that are accelerating
(dynamics) and those that are in equilibrium (statics).

Statics and Dynamics
Dynamics describes the manner in which forces lead to motion of bodies, resulting in
acceleration. Statics describes bodies in equilibrium. For equilibrium, bodies are
motionless or move at a constant velocity. Statics is a subset of dynamics pertaining to
the special case in which acceleration is equal to zero. Dynamics is divided into two
fields: kinematics, the study of the manner in which objects move, and kinetics, the study
of the relationship between forces and motion. Newton’s laws of motion are the
foundation of dynamics.
Newton’s Laws of Motion
Newton’s first law—A body at rest remains at rest, and a body in motion remains in motion at
constant velocity, unless a net external force acts on the body.
Newton’s second law—The acceleration of a body is in the same direction and directly
proportional to the net forces acting on the body and is inversely proportional to the mass of
the body (also known as force is equal to mass multiplied by acceleration).
Newton’s third law—For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
Kinematics

Kinematics is the study of the manner in which objects move—their displacement, velocity,
and acceleration.

Kinematics
Kinematics describes motion but does not provide information about the forces that
lead to motion. Motion can be described as translational or rotational. In three-
dimensional space, six modes, or degrees of freedom, are used to describe motion:
three translational degrees of freedom and three rotational degrees of freedom.
Constraints to movement result in a reduction in the number of degrees of freedom.
Joints of the musculoskeletal system have various amounts of constraint that result in
fewer than six degrees of freedom. For example, in the hip joint, translational motion is
constrained, leaving only three rotational degrees of freedom.
Kinetics
Kinetics is the study of the relationship between forces and motion. Kinetics describes
methods to change motion. Kinetics and mechanics often are used interchangeably in the
discussion of joint mechanics.
Forces can lead to translation or rotation. A force is a push or pull on a body.
A moment (torque) is the rotational equivalent of force. It represents the turning, twisting, or
rotational effect of a force about an axis.
Free-body diagrams are used to visualize the forces and moments acting on the body and to
facilitate analysis of static equilibrium using Newton’s laws of motion.

Kinetics
A force represents an interaction, a push or a pull, on a body. Forces are a vector
quantity because they have a magnitude and a direction. For example, the force of the
quadriceps on the tibia has a force magnitude generated by the quadriceps and acts
along the direction of the quadriceps tendon. Forces cause bodies to initiate motion,
change direction or velocity if already in motion, or change shape (deform). The limbs

9/3/26, 7:30 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004016
3/24

usually are represented as rigid bodies, meaning that they do not deform under load but
may translate, rotate, and apply force. A moment, or torque, represents the manner in
which a force can generate rotational motion. The magnitude of a moment is equal to
the magnitude of a force multiplied by a moment arm, or the shortest distance between
the line of action of a force and the axis of rotation. Skeletal motion results if moments
are applied by muscles that cross the joints on which they act.
Free-body Diagram
Free-body diagrams show all forces and moments acting on a body. They are used to
analyze a system of forces and motion acting on part of the musculoskeletal system.
Equations of equilibrium, following Newton’s second law of motion, are used to predict
unknown forces and moments, such as muscle forces and joint reaction forces, by
balancing the action of known forces and moments, such as body weight from gravity
and other external forces. An example of a free-body diagram is shown in Figure 1.

The quadriceps muscle generates a force (FQuadriceps) to the lower leg and causes a joint

lower leg showing each force as an arrow, with the head of the arrow pointing in the
direction of the applied force. D, The quadriceps muscle creates a counterclockwise
movement (MQuadriceps) to resist the clockwise moments from the weight of the lower
leg (MWLeg) and ankle weight (MExt). (Reproduced with permission from Gustafson JA,
Takenaga T, Debski RE: Basic concepts in functional biomechanics, in Musahl V, Karlsson

Joint Mechanics
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:30 AM

5/24

The structural anatomy of joints provides constraints that lead to mobility along with stability
in various degrees of freedom.
Joints are subject to internal and external loads.

Joint Mechanics
The analysis of joint mechanics involves describing their motion (kinematics) and
loading. External and internal loads act on joints. External loads consist of contact forces
from objects contacting the body, gravitational forces, and forces from inertia. Internal
forces are the response of the body to external forces. Contributors include muscles,
ligaments, and joint contact forces. Joint contact forces are three-dimensional vector
quantities. Often, the magnitude of the joint contact force vector is reported, termed the
joint reaction force.
Hip Biomechanics

Hip Biomechanics
The hip is a ball-in-socket joint, constrained from translational motion but free to rotate
about all three axes of three-dimensional space (three degrees of freedom). Because of
the high articular conformity from the femoral head and the acetabulum, acetabular
labrum, and hip joint capsule, the hip joint is inherently stable while allowing for
rotational motion. The joint reaction force at the hip may exceed multiple body weights,
depending on the activity. Hip motions and loads during gait analysis may reflect internal
tissue response, indicating the state of functional health (Figure 2; Resource 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004016
6/24

Figure 2 Illustrations show a ball-and-socket joint, which has a ball-shaped surface of
one rigid body fitting into a cup-shaped depression of a second rigid body. A ball-and-
socket joint has three degrees of freedom (ie, rotation about three orthogonal axes). The
hip joint is a ball-and-socket joint. (Reproduced from Kaufman K: Biomechanics of the
skeletal system, in Aaron RK, ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science: Foundations of Clinical
Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 39-
49.)
Hip Anatomy
Bony anatomy—the hip joint is the articulation between the femur and pelvis. Three-
dimensional bony morphology may vary widely among individuals (Resource 4).
Variability includes the coverage of the femoral head by the acetabulum; the offset, length,
and orientation of the femoral head-neck junction; and the orientation and depth of the
acetabulum.
The femoral head is not perfectly spherical, and the socket is horseshoe shaped.
The center of the femoral head moves slightly within the socket so the biomechanical
description of the hip as a ball-and-socket joint is an approximation.
Acetabular labrum—the acetabular labrum is a horseshoe-shaped tissue composed of
fibrocartilage with collagen fibers oriented circumferentially around the horseshoe. The
labrum has a triangular cross-section in which the base of the triangular cross-section lies
along the acetabular rim. The acetabular labrum is continuous with the acetabular articular
cartilage.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004016
7/24

Biomechanical function—the acetabular labrum creates a deeper socket in the hip joint and
a suction seal around the hip joint, which adds stability and protects articular cartilage. The
deeper socket also helps retain joint fluid within the acetabulum to aid in lubrication
between the articular cartilage of the femoral head and the acetabulum.
The function and anatomy of the acetabular labrum are similar to that of the glenoid labrum.
Articular cartilage—the thickness of articular cartilage varies throughout the surfaces of the
femoral head and the acetabular cup. Articular cartilage generally is thickest posteriorly and
superiorly on the acetabulum, the locations of the greatest weight-bearing forces.
Capsule and ligaments—external fibers of the capsule are composed of the iliofemoral
ligament, ischiofemoral ligament, and pubofemoral ligament. Internal fibers of the capsule
form a collar around the femoral neck called the zona orbicularis. Fibers spiral around the joint
from the acetabular attachments to the femoral neck near the lesser trochanter. This spiral
arrangement provides stability to the joint. The ligamentum teres is the round ligament of the
femur that attaches the femoral head to the acetabulum. It may function to provide stability.
More than 20 muscles span the hip joint. Grouped according to main function they include the
following:
Abductors and internal rotators: gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fascia lata
Flexors: iliacus, psoas, pectineus, rectus femoris, sartorius, iliocapsularis
Adductors: adductor magnus, adductor brevis, adductor longus, gracilis
Extensors: semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris (long head), gluteus maximus
External rotators: piriformis, obturator externus, obturator internus, superior gemellus,
inferior gemellus, quadratus femoris

Hip Anatomy
The functional groups above categorize muscles by their main function; however,
because of the anatomic location of the hip joint, muscles have multiple functions. For
example, the gluteus maximus extends and externally rotates the hip. The function of a
given muscle also often depends on the orientation of the hip (ie, extended or flexed).
Hip Joint Kinematics
Range of Motion at the Hip Joint
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004016
8/24

Sagittal plane range of motion typically is approximately 130° and may exceed 145° if the knee
is in flexion (Resource 5).
Frontal plane range of motion is approximately 70°.
Transverse plane range of motion is approximately 50°.

Range of Motion at the Hip Joint
The hip joint has a large range of motion. In the sagittal plane, typical range of motion is
from 120° of flexion to 10° of extension. If the knee is flexed, hip range of motion may
exceed 145°. In the frontal plane, typically the hip joint can abduct to 45° and adduct to
25°. In the transverse plane, the hip can internally rotate to 15° and externally rotate to
35°.1
Kinematics During Gait
Dynamic range of motion of the hip during gait does not reach full hip range of motion.
Dynamic range of motion is large in all three planes during gait.
Patterns of hip flexion-extension motion are reproducible among the normal population.

Kinematics During Gait
One gait cycle begins with an initial heel strike and ends with a second heel strike of the
same foot. The gait cycle is composed of stance and swing phases. The stance phase is
the period in which the foot is in contact with the ground, whereas the swing phase is
the period in which the foot is not in contact with the ground. The end of the stance
phase (beginning of the swing phase) is termed toe off. The stance phase accounts for
approximately 60% of the gait cycle, and the swing phase accounts for approximately
40% of the gait cycle. During a gait cycle, the sagittal plane arc of rotation ranges from
approximately 35° of flexion and 10° of extension2 (Figure 3). Hip motion smoothly
cycles from flexion at heel strike to peak extension before toe off, reaching peak flexion
during the swing phase of gait. The frontal plane arc of rotation is approximately 15°

9/3/26, 7:30 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004016
9/24

during the gait cycle. The transverse plane arc of rotation is approximately 20° during
the gait cycle.
Figure 3 Charts show sagittal (A), frontal (B), and transverse (C) plane hip movements
between healthy (solid line), moderate (dotted line), and severe (dashed line) hip
osteoarthritis (OA) groups in which flexion, adduction, and internal rotation are positive
angles. The shaded region represents 1 standard deviation above and below the healthy
group waveform, and the vertical line represents toe off. (Reproduced with permission
from Rutherford DJ, Moreside J, Wong I: Hip joint motion and gluteal muscle activation
differences between healthy controls and those with varying degrees of hip
osteoarthritis during walking. J Electromyogr Kinesiol 2015;25[6]:944-950.)
Kinematics of Pathologic Hips
Patients adopt various walking patterns in response to injury or disease, and the nature of the
adaptation may influence clinical outcome.
Pathologic conditions, such as hip osteoarthritis and femoroacetabular impingement, lead to
kinematic gait disturbances.
Observation of kinematic gait disturbances provides insight into the pathomechanics of these
conditions and provides a basis for evaluating treatment outcomes.
Gait disturbances may cause fatigue during walking because the pattern of gait is no longer
programmed to optimize energy consumption but rather to adapt to the specific nature of the
pathologic condition.

Kinematics of Pathologic Hips
SEND FEEDBACK

10/24

Patients with hip osteoarthritis have a decreased dynamic range of motion compared
with healthy individuals. Patients with hip osteoarthritis also may have a consistent
disturbance in the normal smooth pattern of hip flexion during gait. The disturbance is
characterized by a hesitation or reversal in the direction of sagittal plane motion as the
hip is extended in the middle of the stance phase of gait. In a cohort, 74% of patients
with hip osteoarthritis had the reversal compared with only 5% of healthy individuals.3
The gait adaptations in the patients with hip osteoarthritis were related to pain and
limitations in passive motion. Many of the features of the adaptations were subtle and
not detectable via visual observation alone. Interestingly, patients with femoroacetabular
impingement also had a similar pattern of hip motion during gait compared with
patients with hip osteoarthritis.4
A hip joint contracture may lead to altered posture and kinematics during gait. With
flexion contractures of the hip, lumbar lordosis increases to compensate. Knee flexion
occurs to maintain the position of the center of mass over the feet for stability. A knee
flexion contracture often is associated with a concurrent hip flexion contracture. A
crouched posture results in high-energy demands because the hip, knee, and ankle
extensors must be active continuously to maintain an upright posture. This limits the
time and distance an individual is able to walk. Weakness of the hip flexors limits limb
advancement during the swing phase, resulting in a shortened step length.
Surface Motion
Motion between the surfaces of the hip joint is gliding.
Gliding occurs in all three planes, corresponding to the three degrees of freedom.
In pathologic situations, such as cam-type femoroacetabular impingement, an aspheric
femoral head may cause gliding that is incongruent, resulting in abnormal cartilage
compression.
Hip Joint Mechanics
The force through the hip joint (hip joint contact force) depends on specific factors, such as the
position of the center of gravity, offset of the femoral head from the shaft of the femur, and the

femoral neck-shaft angle.5
Forces at the Hip Joint
Magnitude of force is dependent on activity, ranging from 0.65 to 2.6 times body weight for
typical daily activities6,7 (Table 1).
Contributors to force include muscles, ligaments, and joint shape.
Force from the abductor muscles creates a force across the hip joint, even during the swing
phase of gait, in which the foot is not in contact with the ground and the weight of the body is
not applied to the hip.


Forces at the Hip Joint
The only method to measure in vivo forces at the hip joint is via instrumented total hip
replacement. Data on 15 subjects who underwent total hip arthroplasty instrumented
with the use of force transducers provided valuable information about the forces at the
hip joint.6 Table 1 lists typical forces at the hip joint during daily activities.8 Because only
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004016
12/24

a few patients have an instrumented total hip implant, biomechanical analyses, such as
static equilibrium, are used to predict forces at the hip joint.
Moments at the Hip Joint

Moments at the Hip Joint
Moments occur at the hip joint because of external and internal forces that are applied
at a point of action that is offset from the femoral head. The shortest distance from the
center of the femoral head to the line of action of the force is called the moment arm.
Analogous to forces at the hip joint, moments can be categorized into external and
internal moments. External moments about the hip occur because of the position of the
center of gravity and the point of contact of the body with the environment (such as
foot-ground contact during gait analysis), acting at a distance away from the center of
the femoral head (the hip joint center). These external moments are balanced by internal
moments from muscles, ligaments, and contact between the articular surfaces of the
joint. Ligaments and contact forces usually are neglected in moment analysis of the hip
joint because they are assumed to act through the center of the femoral head. Forces
acting through the hip joint center have a moment arm equal to zero, and, therefore, a
moment equal to zero. Muscle forces have a line of action that does not cross through
the hip joint center and are responsible for generating large moments about the knee
joint.
Static Equilibrium of the Hip
Can be used to predict the combined forces acting on the hip joint using Newton’s second law
For static equilibrium, all forces (F) and moments (M) acting on the hip joint sum to zero:
Net zero sum of forces represents translational equilibrium, and net zero sum of moments
represents rotational equilibrium.
Static equilibrium can be performed in two or three dimensions.

Static Equilibrium of the Hip
For example, in two-dimensional static equilibrium for single-limb stance (Figure 4), the

ground reaction force is 120 lb. The weight of the lower leg is 15% of body weight, or 18

and the hip joint reaction force is unknown. Because the hip joint reaction force is
unknown, unknown reaction forces Rx and Ry are drawn on the free-body diagram in the
positive x-direction and positive y-direction, respectively. After the equilibrium equations
are solved, if the value is negative, the reaction force points in the opposite direction.

Because the hip abductor force has a small moment arm about the hip joint, the hip
joint reaction force is larger than the abductor force.
The Hip as a Fulcrum
The hip joint acts as a fulcrum, or the balancing point between body weight and abductor
muscles.
An increase in femoral offset (perpendicular distance from the center of the femoral head to
the anatomic axis of the femur) correlates with a decrease in abductor force requirements,
decreasing joint reaction forces.
Hip muscle weakness influences the forces and motions at the hip joint by changing the
balance between muscle forces and body weight.
Patients may compensate for pain or other pathology by changing the fulcrum point with
posture changes, which has a large influence on hip joint mechanics.

The Hip as a Fulcrum
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Hip

The aforementioned example illustrates the manner in which the hip joint acts as a
fulcrum, balancing body weight and the pull of the abductor muscles. For single-limb
stance, simple biomechanical calculations showed that the hip joint reaction force was
larger than body weight and oriented in almost the same direction as the hip abductor
muscle force. Similar analyses can be performed for other body poses. For two-leg
stance, the hip joint reaction force is approximately two-thirds of body weight (Table 1).
A neutral two-leg standing posture can be maintained at the hip with relatively little
muscle activity; forces increase at the hip joint only if slight perturbations lead to hip
joint positions slightly out of neutral.
Femoral Offset
Femoral offset is the perpendicular distance from the center of the femoral head to the
anatomic axis of the femur.
Acetabular offset is the horizontal distance from the center of the femoral head to the pubic
symphysis midline.
Global offset is the combined femoral and acetabular offset.9

Femoral Offset
Femoral offset, or the perpendicular distance from the center of the femoral head to the
anatomic axis of the femur, contributes to the moment arm of the abductor muscles
about the hip joint. Increasing femoral offset increases the moment arm and mechanical
advantage of the abductor muscles about the hip joint center, and the abductor muscles
can use less force to produce the same moment. The net result at the hip joint is a
decrease in hip joint reaction force. This has implications for restoring femoral offset and
global offset after total hip arthroplasty. Restoring femoral offset helps optimize hip
abductor muscle function by keeping the hip abductor muscle moment arm at the
appropriate length. If femoral offset is reduced, the hip abductor muscle moment arm
has less mechanical advantage and would require additional force to apply the same
moment to the hip joint. The result is a disruption in joint stability, increases in hip joint
reaction force, and possible mechanical consequences for the implant.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004016
18/24

Gait and Posture Adaptations

Gait and Posture Adaptations
Other factors that lead to altered loading at the hip joint include movement adaptations
to avoid pain. With a painful hip, a patient may lean the trunk laterally over the painful
leg during stance. This moves the center of mass of the body closer to directly above the
hip joint center, reducing the need for contraction of the hip abductor muscles to
counteract body weight. The net reaction is that compressive forces decrease across the
joint, reducing pain. In a similar manner, weakness of the hip abductors also results in
increased lateral trunk lean to the side of weakness as the patient shifts the center of
mass toward the weak side. This results in a Trendelenburg gait, in which the pelvis dips
to the contralateral side because the hip abductors cannot maintain joint position.
Using a cane on the contralateral side of the painful or weak hip also reduces hip joint
reaction force. The cane creates a second moment to counteract the moment acting on
the hip joint from body weight acting at the center of mass. The amount of hip abductor
muscle contraction necessary is reduced, lowering hip joint reaction force. The moment
arm of the cane to the hip joint center is much larger than the moment arm of the hip
abductor muscles; therefore, even small forces on the cane may substantially reduce the
necessary abductor force.
Muscle Weakness

Muscle Weakness
Moderate and severe weakness of the hip extensors results in increasing modifications
to be able to ambulate. With moderate weakness of the hip extensors, the patient
compensates with forward trunk flexion. Forward trunk flexion places the hip extensors
in a position of increased mechanical advantage. With severe weakness of the hip
extensors, upper-limb assistive devices are necessary to maintain an erect posture.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004016
19/24

Biomechanics of Total Hip Arthroplasty
Kinematics
Walking parameters, including walking velocity, range of motion, and joint moments, may be
affected after total hip arthroplasty.10
Daily activities, such as moving from a sitting position to a standing position and ascending
stairs, also reveal differences between patients who undergo total hip arthroplasty and
healthy control patients but not necessarily more so than level walking.

Kinematics
A systematic review found that almost all studies in the literature have reported reduced
dynamic range of motion during walking after total hip arthroplasty. Hip abduction angle
also may be reduced.11 The combined effect is a shift of the center of mass over the
implanted limb. This may be because of compensatory measures to avoid pain that was
present preoperatively or to provide more stability to the hip joint. Although differences
were observed in other activities, such as ascending stairs, the differences between
patients who underwent total hip arthroplasty and healthy control patients were not
greater than those observed for level walking.
Bearing Surface Motion
Surface motion at the artificial hip is sliding within the ball-and-socket of the replaced femoral
head and the acetabular cup.
Sliding under hip joint loading leads to abrasive/adhesive polyethylene wear of acetabular
cups.
Impingement, or contact between an unintended surface, such as the femoral neck and the
acetabular cup, can occur because the dynamic range of motion of the hip during various daily
activities is greater than that that accommodated by the hip implant.

The hip joint center should be restored after total hip arthroplasty for normal gait and
function.
Femoral offset and global offset restoration are essential to avoid complications after total hip
arthroplasty.
Limb-length equality must be maintained while not sacrificing hip stability.
The range of motion allowed by a particular total hip construct is directly related to the ratio
between the diameter of the femoral head and the diameter of the femoral neck.
Large heads with thinner femoral necks are less likely to result in impingement, subluxation,
and dislocation. Dislocation risk also is driven by acetabular component orientation.

Implant Design and Placement
Implant selection and placement are critical to restore hip joint biomechanics and
maintain femoral offset and leg length. Reconstruction of femoral offset is critical for
preventing impingement, hip instability, polyethylene wear, and trochanteric pain.12
Analogous to nonimplanted hip biomechanics, hip implant stems that have a larger
femoral offset create a larger hip abductor muscle moment arm, which may decrease
the hip joint reaction force; however, greater offset increases soft-tissue tension, which
may lead to trochanteric pain. Decreased femoral offset may increase hip joint reaction
forces, hip instability, and abductor weakness. Femoral offset can be adjusted via hip
component and placement choices (eg, increasing the length of the femoral neck,
decreasing the neck-shaft angle, or medializing the femoral head while increasing neck
length increase femoral offset).12 Another consideration is correction of leg-length
inequality while maintaining hip stability. Hip arthroplasty patients with symptomatic leg-
length inequality have reduced dynamic range of motion. Leg length is determined
primarily by the femoral component position and neck length and secondarily by the
acetabular component position.
Other design factors also are important in the biomechanics of total hip arthroplasty.
The ratio between the diameter of the femoral head and the diameter of the femoral
neck dictates the range of motion allowed by a particular implant (in considering
implants with the same cup entrance plane). As the femoral component rotates within
the hip toward the end of the allowed range of motion, it may impinge on the acetabular

component or the pelvis. Recurrent impingement may lead to component damage or
instability because of subluxation and dislocation. Dislocation risk is decreased with
larger head sizes; however, head size is not the only factor that influences dislocation
risk. Acetabular cup orientation, specifically acetabular cups oriented far from 45° of
inclination from the coronal plane and 15° of anteversion, are more likely to dislocate.
Larger head sizes, with smaller-diameter femoral necks, theoretically allow for increased
range of motion before impingement but with tradeoffs. Larger heads apply higher
frictional moments that increase the forces on fixation interfaces of the implant,
influencing cup loosening and taper corrosion.13 Although modern materials have
largely eliminated this problem, if adhesive/abrasive polyethylene wear is a concern,
larger head sizes result in longer sliding distances at the bearing surfaces and higher
wear rates.
